Slay the Spire relies heavily on luck. Two runs can be similar but aren't the same. There's a lot riding on your first Act because it doesn't matter what build you want to play, there's either going to be a build you get to play or a death if you don't make it come together. Along with deck order being pre-determined as a fight starts(a wise move to prevent save scumming, just noting the mechanic) it's a management game long term more than anything. In order to be truly good at the game, you need hours and hours and dozens and dozens of runs for true progress. Because the game is geared on that it really feels more like I'm zoning out hoping for a good run or managing a dead run mid to late game. While it does excel at small rewards to keep the player invested including progress on death I won't pretend it's a style of gameplay I'm super into. But for it's genre I think it's done very well.

This isn't my genre but I think it excels at what it wants and if you get it on sale specifically you'll be pleased for at least your first dozens runs.

Tips and tricks for the interested:

-Large decks are usually a trap, burying the best cards or your intended build under energy wasters. 15-20 cards or less is my advice

-I almost always try to gun for Events and Rests over Elites after Act 1

-During Rests, if you can, I'd recommend upgrading cards. Specifically any beyond the basic Defense and Attack you start with

-Avoid bias with your deck and adapt. Re-evaluating even endgame can help win your fights, and never expect to get the exact build you are looking for

In comparison to the second game wise, Ironclad's and Defect's kits feels similar but still distinctly different, silent is comparable between the two games although game context makes it feel different. Watcher, Necrobinder and Regent are completely different experiences altogether. 
The only thing really feeling missed in the first game is the multiplayer aspect of the second, but even then there are mods which can achieve similar thing.

All that being said, STS1 and STS2 are both excellent games which i've put hundreds of hours combined and would reccomend getting both if able to experience the difference in design philosophy between the two games

The other benchmark. FTL and this one are the two games I hold every roguelike up against, and most of what comes out does not make it. People call this a deckbuilder and it is, but I think that undersells it. It is a decision game. The cards are just how the decisions show up.

What Slay the Spire understands, and what most of its imitators never do, is that every card you take is a bet on where the run is going. Not a bonus. A bet. Take the big attack and you are committing to a deck that wants to end fights fast and you had better find the draw to support it. Skip it and you are saying you trust the defense you have not found yet. Fifteen floors later, that one pick is the reason you won or the reason you are staring at the heart with no answer, and here is the part that matters. The game is clear enough that you always know which pick it was. You never lose to something you could not have seen. You lose because you made a bet and it did not come in, and you can trace the line back to the exact floor where you made it. That clarity is rare. It is the whole reason the game is replayable, because every loss is a lesson instead of an excuse.

The other thing it gets right is that nothing in it is wasted. Every character is a different game with the same rules. Ironclad plays like a brawl, Silent plays like a trap, Defect plays like an engine, Watcher plays like you are holding a loaded gun the entire fight. The relic system means that even two runs with the same deck plan feel completely different, because the relics are what change the math. And the ascension ladder is the best difficulty system I have seen in anything. It does not make enemies spongier. It takes things away from you, one at a time, until the run you used to cruise through becomes a real fight again. There is always a next ascension and there is always a reason to go for it.

There is no story to speak of and it does not need one. The run is the story. You remember the run where you found the one relic that turned a dead deck into a monster. You remember the run where you had the heart at ten health and drew the wrong card. Those are the stories and they are better than most games manage with a script.

Honest criticism. The art is functional and that is being generous. The game is a decade old and it looks it. And if you do not like thinking three turns ahead you will not like this, because that is the entire game and there is no mode that lets you skip it.
